input.question: Salts are constantly added to the ocean through volcanic emissions, runoff from continents, and the weathering of rocks in general, but is there any process that reverses this and removes it?
input.ground_truth: Yes. Salt can settle out, be captured by organic processes, and (most commonly) become landlocked. In that last one, a part of the ocean recedes or gets cut off from the rest of the ocean. The water evaporates and deposits the salt (which gets buried over time), then the fresh water rains back into the rest of the ocean.

Okay! Imagine the ocean is like a big bathtub. Every day, some salt "grains" (from volcanoes, rocks, and land) fall into the bathtub. But the bathtub doesn't just keep filling up with salt forever, right?

So, how does the salt leave the bathtub? Well, it happens very slowly! Some salt gets stuck in the shells of tiny ocean animals, like clams and snails. When these animals die, their shells sink to the bottom of the ocean. Over a very, very long time, those shells turn into rock, and the salt is trapped inside. That’s one way salt leaves the water and goes into the ground.

Also, a little bit of salt can get stuck in the mud or sand at the bottom of the ocean, and then, when that mud or sand becomes rock, the salt stays there too.

So, the ocean doesn’t get saltier and saltier forever because some of the salt gets trapped in the ground or in shells over a looooong time!
